title: How Ananse Won the Sky God’s Stories

pages.text: Long ago, all the stories in the world belonged to Nyame, the sky god. Ananse the spider climbed up to the sky and asked for them. “What price will you pay for my stories?” Nyame asked.
sentences: Long ago, all the stories in the world belonged to Nyame, the sky god.
Ananse the spider climbed up to the sky and asked for them.
“What price will you pay for my stories?” Nyame asked.
pages.alt: Small clever Ananse the spider standing on a wispy cloud looking up respectfully at the majestic, kindly Sky God Nyame in golden kente robes among radiant clouds.

pages.text: Nyame set four hard tasks. “Bring me Onini the python, the Mmoboro hornets, Osebo the leopard, and Mmoatia the fairy,” he said. Some storytellers change this list a little.
sentences: “Bring me Onini the python, the Mmoboro hornets, Osebo the leopard, and Mmoatia the fairy,” he said.
Some storytellers change this list a little.
pages.alt: Nyame the Sky God among golden clouds holding up four fingers clearly while small Ananse listens attentively below.

pages.text: Ananse went home and asked his wife, Aso, for help. In many tellings, she gives clever advice. Together they made a smart plan, because two minds are better than one.
sentences: Ananse went home and asked his wife, Aso, for help.
In many tellings, she gives clever advice.
Together they made a smart plan, because two minds are better than one.
pages.alt: Ananse and his thoughtful wife Aso sitting together at a wooden table inside their cosy home with a calabash gourd and woven vine, smiling as they plan.

pages.text: One by one, in the story, Ananse tricked each creature and carried them up to the sky. This is only a tale. Nobody should ever trap real snakes, hornets, or leopards. They are dangerous, and they belong in the wild.
sentences: One by one, in the story, Ananse tricked each creature and carried them up to the sky.
Nobody should ever trap real snakes, hornets, or leopards.
They are dangerous, and they belong in the wild.
pages.alt: Ananse climbing a glowing stairway of clouds toward the sky carrying a closed woven basket and gourd, while far below in the lush green forest wild animals roam free and undisturbed.

pages.text: Nyame was amazed. “You have done everything I asked,” he said. “From today, the stories are yours, and they shall be called Spider Stories.”
sentences: “You have done everything I asked,” he said.
“From today, the stories are yours, and they shall be called Spider Stories.”
pages.alt: Nyame smiling warmly among the clouds and handing a glowing golden carved wooden story-box to joyful Ananse.

pages.text: That is why many Akan people call folktales Anansesem, or spider stories. When elders tell them in the evening, children gather round to listen and learn.
sentences: That is why many Akan people call folktales Anansesem, or spider stories.

pages.alt: A Ghanaian village elder seated by a warm evening courtyard fire telling an animated story while happy children sit on mats listening in wonder under starry skies.
